02One team, one story

Realpage + Cherre: one unified message

Blueprint is the first major industry event since Realpage acquired Cherre, and the first time the two brands appear together in public. Decision Intelligence is the Realpage group that brings the legacy Data & Analytics team and the incoming Cherre business unit together as one product and service line, and everyone attending, across Decision Intelligence and every other Realpage team on-site, is telling the same story.

Decision Intelligence, Smart Building, and Realpage Exchange, showing up at Blueprint as one presence, not two separate booths.

Our story in one sentence

We help real estate organizations build the trusted data foundation that enables better decisions today and prepares them for AI tomorrow.

The narrative, in order

  1. The industry has changed. More data, faster technology adoption, and AI investment happening all at once.
  2. The challenge isn’t more data. It’s confidence in the data organizations already have.
  3. Trusted data creates better decisions. Quality, connection, and governance are what make analytics and AI usable.
  4. Better decisions create better outcomes. Efficiency, visibility, faster investment decisions, confident AI adoption.

The conversation, at three lengths

30 seconds

“What do Realpage and Cherre do together?”

Realpage and Cherre bring trusted, connected data to real estate organizations. By improving quality, governance, and visibility, we help clients decide better today and get ready for AI tomorrow.

60 seconds

“Tell me more.”

The industry is racing toward AI, but most organizations are still fighting fragmented systems and manual processes. We solve those foundational problems first, so clients get stronger reporting and more confidence in every decision, while building what they’ll need for AI.

Three minutes

Start with their problem, not our platform.

Ask: “What operational challenge is taking your team the longest to solve today?” Listen first, understand the business challenge, and only then explain how trusted information supports better decisions.

Trusted data, made visible: what the platform behind the story looks like in the room.

Five message pillars

Pillar one
Trusted data
Pillar two
AI readiness
Pillar three
Decision Intelligence
Pillar four
Connected operations
Pillar five
Confidence

Messaging do’s and don’ts

Do

Lead with the client’s problem

Business outcomes over technical features, plain language, thoughtful questions, and bring in another teammate when it helps.

Don’t

Lead with product names

Skip straight to a demo, assume everyone knows the org chart, overuse jargon, or treat it like a pitch.

Questions you’ll hear

Realpage recognized that trusted, connected data has become foundational to the future of AI and real estate technology. Bringing Cherre together with Decision Intelligence strengthens the ability to help clients build confidence in their data while expanding what’s possible across the broader Realpage platform. Avoid framing this as Cherre needing rescue, or as Realpage simply buying technology; the story is about creating more value for clients, not one company replacing another.

No. Cherre continues to play a critical role within Decision Intelligence and remains the trusted data foundation behind many of the capabilities on display at Blueprint. What’s changed is the ability to bring those capabilities to clients as part of a much broader Realpage platform.

AI is creating real opportunity across the industry, but it is only as valuable as the information behind it. The focus here is helping organizations build trusted, connected data so AI produces meaningful, reliable outcomes, not just faster answers.

04How to work the floor

The booth playbook

Every visitor is the start of a story, not a badge scan. This is the practical layer: how to open a conversation, read who you’re talking to, and close with a real next step.

The client journey, five steps

1

Curiosity

Something catches their eye. The goal is to earn a slow-down, not a sale.

2

Engagement

Start a conversation, not a presentation. “What caught your eye?” “What brought you to Blueprint this year?” Encourage them to take (and post) a selfie in the space.

3

Discovery

Only after rapport, explore the business challenge: what initiative is taking the longest, where are they investing, how are they thinking about AI.

4

Connection

Think about who else on the team would strengthen the conversation, and make the introduction before they ask.

5

Next step

A demo, an introduction, an executive meeting, a LinkedIn connection. Never let a good conversation just end.

Action

The first sixty seconds decide whether someone feels sold to or welcomed. Skip “what company are you with?” Try “what brought you to Blueprint?” or “what’s been the most interesting thing you’ve seen today?”

Reading the room

Five visitor types and how to meet each one.
VisitorWhat to do
The explorerLet them look around. Ask what caught their attention. Don’t interrupt discovery.
The shopperAsk questions, understand priorities, introduce the right expert.
The existing clientCelebrate the relationship. Introduce colleagues they haven’t met. Ask what’s changed.
The partnerLearn what they’re hearing in the market. Introduce Jacob or Matt when it fits.
The executiveKeep it strategic. Focus on business outcomes. Bring in leadership early.

Common mistakes

  • Talking more than the client
  • Explaining products before understanding the problem
  • Trying to answer everything yourself instead of introducing a teammate
  • Rushing to a demo before it’s the right next step
  • Forgetting to write down what mattered

The warm introduction

Three parts: context (“Cris, I’d like you to meet Sarah”), the reason you’re connecting them (“we were discussing building systems, and I thought your perspective would help”), and staying in the conversation instead of disappearing once the introduction is made.

If the booth is busy

Prioritize quality over quantity

Acknowledge anyone waiting, smile, and offer the library or Book Club while a teammate becomes free. Nobody should feel ignored.

If the booth is quiet

That’s not downtime

Whoever’s covering the booth stays put; everyone else can walk the floor, visit partners, attend sessions, support teammates, or capture content. Blueprint happens beyond Booth 320, but the booth is never empty.

Requirement

The booth must be manned at all times during expo hours. This isn’t optional. The onsite team is responsible for coordinating coverage among themselves, using the discipline above: if it’s busy, don’t let anyone stand alone; if it’s quiet, that’s still someone’s shift, not a reason to leave it empty.

05Your voice matters

Social media playbook

A photo from a teammate will almost always outperform a polished corporate graphic. The goal is fifteen employee posts across the event, not because we’re chasing impressions, but because people trust people.

Action

The social media calendar lives in the Blueprint master tracker and updates as the event approaches: open the tracker. Check it before posting if you want to slot into a planned theme rather than post cold.

What to share, before, during, and after

Before Blueprint

Anticipation

What you’re looking forward to, who you’re hoping to meet, why this year matters.

During Blueprint

The experience

The booth, the Book Club, coffee cups, team photos, roundtables, and client conversations without confidential detail.

After Blueprint

Reflection

Your biggest takeaway, a favorite conversation, an industry trend, or a new relationship.

Hashtags and tagging

Every post should include #NextChapter, and every post should tag @Realpage and @Cherre, no exceptions. Add event hashtags where they fit: #Blueprint2026, #BlueprintVegas, #PropTech, #RealEstateTechnology. Tag clients when appropriate, partners, speakers, and teammates, but only when they’re genuinely part of the story, not to inflate reach.

Brand voice, one example

Instead of

“Excited to showcase our innovative AI-powered solutions.”

Reads like a press release.

Try

“One of my favorite conversations today was about something simple: trust.”

Sounds like a person. Focus on what you learned, not what you sold.

Do’s and don’ts

Do

Share, celebrate, engage

Authentic observations, teammates’ wins, client conversations kept confidential where needed, and comments on other employees’ posts.

Don’t

Confidential detail, badges, pitches

No confidential client information, no photographed badges, no private meeting notes, no announcing deals early, no turning every post into a pitch.

Before you post a photo, ask

  • Is everyone comfortable being photographed?
  • Are names or confidential materials visible?
  • Does this represent the brand well?
  • Does it tell a story?
  • Would you be proud to see it on LinkedIn tomorrow?
  • Did you tag @Realpage and @Cherre?
  • Did you use #NextChapter?

What counts as a qualified conversation

Not every interaction is one. Generally it means we understand the organization’s current priorities, we identified a business challenge, we know who owns that initiative, we established a logical next step, or we connected with the right decision maker. “Nice meeting you” isn’t enough. “Let’s continue this next week” is.

Four priorities

One

Strengthen existing relationships

Deepen what already exists through face-to-face time and executive engagement.

Two

Advance active opportunities

Remove obstacles, bring in expertise, validate priorities, agree on next steps.

Three

Identify new opportunities

Not everyone arrives to buy. Stay curious and listen for what emerges naturally.

Four

Strengthen the partner ecosystem

Partner conversations count as much as client ones.

Discovery framework

Understand (“what initiatives is your team focused on this year?”) → Explore (“what’s making that difficult today?”) → Clarify (“how are you solving that now?”) → Expand (“who else is involved?”) → Connect (“I’d love to introduce you to someone on our team”) → Confirm (“would it make sense to continue this after Blueprint?”).

09Ownership, not attendance

Your responsibilities + expectations

Everyone reading this, whether you’re on the floor, managing someone who is, or reading this on the way to the airport, owns a piece of what Blueprint is supposed to accomplish.

If you’re on the floor

Represent one team

Lead with curiosity, bring in the right expert, log what you learn, and leave every interaction a little better than you found it.

If you manage someone attending

Set the expectation before they land

Make sure they’ve read sections 01, 02, and 04 through 06 before the flight, and that they know what a qualified conversation looks like.

If you’re reading this back at your desk

You’re still part of the story

Engage with teammates’ posts, follow up on introductions made on your behalf, and help close what gets logged in Salesforce.

Business development isn’t one team’s responsibility. It’s shared by everyone in the room.

Built for the Decision Intelligence team attending Blueprint 2026. Presented by Jess Timmerman, Kathy Raissifar, and Keren Cordon.
